steps.title: The numerical parameters and their elementary bounds
steps.body:
Claim. Under the displayed restrictions, \(\beta>0\), \(\kappa\ge1\), \(0\le q<1\), \(h\le1/\beta\), and \(B\ge0\).

Proof. Since \(\beta\ge\alpha>0\), division by \(\alpha\) preserves \(\beta\ge\alpha\) and gives \(\kappa\ge1\). Multiplication by \(h\ge0\) gives \(\alpha h\le\beta h\le1\), so \(q\ge0\). The strict inequality \(\alpha h>0\) gives \(q<1\). Dividing \(h\beta\le1\) by \(\beta>0\) gives the step restriction. Finally \(h>0\) and the nonnegativity of the square root imply \(B\ge0\).

steps.title: The first-order potential contract and the original Hessian bounds
steps.body:
Definition. On a real inner product space, the potential contract requires \(V\in C^2\), \(\alpha\)-strong convexity and a \( eta\)-Lipschitz gradient:

\[V(y)\ge V(x)+\langle abla V(x),y-x angle+ rac\alpha2\|y-x\|^2,\qquad\| abla V(y)- abla V(x)\|\le eta\|y-x\|.\]

The original source Hessian bounds imply this contract with exactly the same constants, as proved in the Hessian-assumption argument. The contract contains no invariant law, semigroup, spectral basis or comparison conclusion; those objects and properties are constructed separately.

steps.title: Positive contractions and weighted interpolation
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(T\) be a self-adjoint linear operator on a real inner product space with \(0\le\langle x,Tx\rangle\le\|x\|^2\). Then \(\|Tx\|^2\le\langle x,Tx\rangle\). If additionally \(a\|x\|^2\le\langle x,Tx\rangle\le b\|x\|^2\), then

\[\|u-Tu+Tv\|^2\le(1-a)\|u\|^2+b\|v\|^2.\]

Proof. The quadratic function \(F(x)=\langle x,Tx\rangle/2\) has gradient \(Tx\). Positivity and the upper quadratic bound give its convex lower model and unit-smooth upper model. The resulting gradient inequality yields \(\|Tx\|^2\le\langle x,Tx\rangle\). Expanding \(\|u+T(v-u)\|^2\), applying this inequality to \(v-u\), and using symmetry gives the sharper upper bound \(\|u\|^2-\langle u,Tu\rangle+\langle v,Tv\rangle\). The two quadratic-form bounds finish the proof.

For \(T=hA\), where \(A\) is self-adjoint with \(\alpha I\preceq A\preceq\beta I\), the restriction \(h\beta\le1\) supplies \(0\preceq T\preceq I\). Taking \(a=\alpha h\), \(b=\beta h\) gives

\[\|u-hAu+hAv\|^2\le(1-\alpha h)\|u\|^2+h\beta\|v\|^2.\]

steps.title: The shifted identity and the martingale residual constant
steps.body:
Claim. If \(z^+=z-hAz+D\) and \(D=g-g^++M\), then

\[z^++g^+=(z+g)-hA(z+g)+hAg+M.\]

This follows by substituting the two equalities and cancelling the added terms. If \(\langle U,M\rangle=0\), expanding the square gives \(\|U+M\|^2=\|U\|^2+\|M\|^2\).

For any real \(c\), if \(\|D\|^2\le3c\) and \(\|J\|^2\le6c\), then

\[\|D-J\|^2\le18c.\]

Indeed the triangle inequality and \(2ab\le a^2+b^2\) give \(\|D-J\|^2\le2\|D\|^2+2\|J\|^2\le18c\). This is the source's residual constant, derived from its two separate estimates.

steps.title: Conditional expectation supplies the orthogonality
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(U,M\in L^2(Q;H)\), let \(\mathcal G\) be a sub-\(\sigma\)-algebra, suppose \(U\) is \(\mathcal G\)-measurable and \(\mathbb E[M\mid\mathcal G]=0\). Then \(\langle U,M\rangle_{L^2}=0\). In particular, if \(\|U\|_{L^2}^2\le qE+\ell\), then

\[\|U+M\|_{L^2}^2\le qE+\ell+\|M\|_{L^2}^2.\]

Proof. Conditional expectation is the orthogonal projection onto the closed subspace of \(\mathcal G\)-measurable square-integrable vectors. Hence \(\langle M,U\rangle=\langle\mathbb E[M\mid\mathcal G],U\rangle=0\). Symmetry of the real inner product gives the claimed orientation. Substitute this equality into the squared-norm expansion and apply the predictable energy bound.

\[h=\frac1\beta\min\left(1,\frac{\varepsilon}{12\sqrt d}\right), \qquad K=\frac\beta\alpha\max\left(1,\frac{12\sqrt d}{\varepsilon}\right).\]

The constants \(6\) and \(12\), the maximum, minimum and logarithm are the literal quantities of Corollary 1.1. A convergence estimate for actual sampling laws is not established by this scalar argument.

steps.title: The transient estimate and the complete scalar accuracy bound
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(0<t\le1\), \(A\ge0\), \(\varepsilon>0\). If \(k\) is a natural number with \(\log(1+2A/\varepsilon)\le tk\), then

\[(1-t)^kA\le\varepsilon/2.\]

Proof. Since \(1-t\le e^{-t}\) and both are nonnegative, \((1-t)^k\le e^{-tk}\). The logarithmic hypothesis gives \(e^{-tk}\le(1+2A/\varepsilon)^{-1}\). Multiplication by \(A\ge0\) yields the result because \(A/(1+2A/\varepsilon)\le\varepsilon/2\). This includes \(A=0\) and \(t=1\).

\[\sqrt\alpha\left((1-\alpha h)^kR+6h\sqrt{(\beta/\alpha)\beta d}\right)\le\varepsilon.\]

steps.title: The independent past, its tail and its newest innovation
steps.body:
Construction. For an innovation probability law \(\eta\), put \(Q=\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N}\) on sequences \(\omega=(\omega_0,\omega_1,\ldots)\). The tail map is \(\tau\omega=(\omega_1,\omega_2,\ldots)\).

Claim. The map \(\tau\) preserves \(Q\), and the tail is independent of \(\omega_0\).

Proof. Every finite set of coordinates has its product law. Reindexing a finite cylinder by the injective successor map therefore leaves its probability unchanged; the product-measure identity gives measure preservation. Independence follows because every finite set of tail coordinates has indices disjoint from \(\{0\}\). Independence of the full tail process follows from these finite-coordinate independence statements.

steps.title: A contraction on the complete space of square-integrable past functions
steps.body:
Construction and claim. Suppose \(F:E\to E\) is \(q\)-Lipschitz with \(0\le q<1\), the innovation has finite second moment, and \(a\in\mathbb R\). On \(L^2(Q;E)\) define

\[\Phi(X)=F(X\circ\tau)+a\omega_0.\]

The tail pullback is a linear isometry because \(\tau\) preserves \(Q\); the head coordinate is square-integrable because its law is \(\eta\). A Lipschitz map has at most linear growth, so composition with \(F\) preserves square integrability on the probability space. The common additive noise cancels in a difference, giving

\[\|\Phi(X)-\Phi(Y)\|_{L^2}\le q\|X\circ\tau-Y\circ\tau\|_{L^2} =q\|X-Y\|_{L^2}.\]

Thus \(\Phi\) is a strict contraction on a complete space.

Claim. The scaled IPLA parameters are

\[\alpha_N=Nm,\qquad\beta_N=NL,\qquad h_N=\frac{\gamma}{N},\qquad d_N=d_\theta+Nd_x.\]

They satisfy \(0<\alpha_N\le\beta_N\), \(h_N>0\), and \(h_N\beta_N\le1\). The finite-sum potential \(V_N\) belongs to \(C^2\).

Proof. Positivity of the particle number and of \(m,\gamma\) gives the strict positive parameters. Multiplying \(m\le L\) by \(N\) gives the curvature ordering. Exact cancellation yields \(h_N\beta_N=\gamma L\le1\). Each map \(z\mapsto(\theta,\sqrt N z_i)\) is continuous linear, so composition with \(U\in C^2\) is twice continuously differentiable; a finite sum preserves this regularity.

steps.title: Projecting the finite transport estimate to the parameter
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\theta^\star\) maximize the latent-integrated density \(\int e^{-U(\theta,x)}\,dx\). For a finite-second-moment probability initialization,

\[\left(\mathbb E_{\mu_k}\|\theta-\theta^\star\|^2\right)^{1/2}\le W_2(\mu_k,\pi_N)+C_N.\]

Proof. The established IPLA concentration theorem gives \((\mathbb E_{\pi_N}\|\theta-\theta^\star\|^2)^{1/2}\le C_N\) from the same joint strong convexity. The parameter projection has operator norm at most one. For any coupling of \(\mu_k\) and \(\pi_N\), the \(L^2\) triangle inequality bounds the projected distance to \(\theta^\star\) by its coupling displacement plus that target radius. Taking the coupling infimum gives the displayed inequality. The coordinate convergence-finiteness theorem proves finite output transport first; this and concentration prove a finite projected second moment before converting the extended moment to the ordinary square-root integral.

steps.title: The linear-step parameter bounds with either initialization distance
steps.body:
Claim. Define \(q=1-m\gamma\in[0,1)\), \(R_h=W_2(\mu_0,\widehat\pi_{N,\gamma})\), and \(R_0=W_2(\mu_0,\pi_N)\). Then the actual IPLA parameter error satisfies both

\[\left(\mathbb E_{\mu_k}\|\theta-\theta^\star\|^2\right)^{1/2}\le C_N+q^kR_h+B_N,\qquad \left(\mathbb E_{\mu_k}\|\theta-\theta^\star\|^2\right)^{1/2}\le C_N+q^kR_0+B_N.\]

Proof. For the invariant-based form, apply the fully constructed lifted Wasserstein comparison and then the parameter-projection inequality. For the target-based form, compare the actual iterates from \(\mu_0\) and \(\pi_N\) by the Gaussian contraction theorem, yielding \(q^kR_0\). The stationary-start Poisson comparison bounds the distance of the second iterate from \(\pi_N\) by \(B_N\). Their transport triangle and the same projection bound give the second formula with only a single bias. The lifted constants simplify exactly to \(q\) and \(B_N\) by the established particle-scaling identities. The supporting uniform corollary with \(2B_N\) follows by weakening this bound using \(B_N\ge0\); it is not required by the sharper target statement.

steps.title: A direct comparison with the complete Project 03 bound
steps.body:
Claim. Under the preceding structural assumptions and the additional comparison regime \(m\gamma\le121/1600\), the new target-based right side is no greater than

\[C_N+q^kW_2(\mu_0,\pi_N)+\frac{33}{20}\frac Lm\sqrt D\sqrt\gamma,\]

the right side used by Project 03 for the same dimensions and initialization.

Proof. The two bounds have the same statistical radius and exactly the same Gibbs-based transient. The only change is the discretization term. The established coefficient inequality \(B_N\le(33/20)(L/m)\sqrt D\sqrt\gamma\) holds throughout the stated regime. Add the unchanged two terms to that inequality and combine it with the new sharp parameter bound. Thus the linear-step estimate gives an explicit improvement for sufficiently small steps; it does not claim to cover the larger step interval or weaker regularity assumptions of every case of Project 03.

steps.title: Explicit normalized accuracy and its iteration count
steps.body:
Claim. Fix \(\varepsilon>0\). Let \(R\) be either \(R_h\) or \(R_0\), matching the desired initialization form. Choose particles and step so that

\[N\varepsilon^2\ge18d_\theta,\qquad \gamma=\frac1{L\max\{1,18\sqrt D/\varepsilon\}}.\]

For every nonnegative integer \(k\) satisfying

\[k\ge\frac Lm\max\!\left\{1,\frac{18\sqrt D}{\varepsilon}\right\}\log\!\left(1+\frac{3\sqrt m\,R}{\varepsilon}\right),\]

the actual parameter law has normalized root-mean-square error at most \(\varepsilon\):

\[\sqrt m\left(\mathbb E_{\mu_k}\|\theta-\theta^\star\|^2\right)^{1/2}\le\varepsilon.\]

Proof. Multiply the corresponding sharp parameter bound by \(\sqrt m\). The concentration scaling identity gives \(\sqrt{2d_\theta/N}\). The scalar accuracy theorem allocates at most \(\varepsilon/3\) to that radius, the logarithmically controlled transient, and the normalized linear bias \(6L\gamma\sqrt D\). The displayed particle budget, step and iteration count are precisely its hypotheses, so their sum is at most \(\varepsilon\). The maximum keeps the step positive even when the effective dimension is zero.

steps.title: The sharp rate for the original independent Gaussian recursion
steps.body:
Claim. Take a square-integrable scaled initial state on an actual probability space and an innovation sequence satisfying IPLA's original coordinatewise standard-Gaussian laws, independence across time and coordinates, and independence from initialization. Under the displayed \(C^2\), joint curvature and step assumptions, the original noise-driven IPLA laws satisfy

\[\left(\mathbb E\|\theta_k-\theta^\star\|^2\right)^{1/2}\le\sqrt{\frac{2d_\theta}{Nm}}+(1-m\gamma)^kW_2(\operatorname{Law}(Z_0),\pi_N)+6\gamma\sqrt{(L/m)L(d_x+d_\theta/N)}.\]

Proof. Assemble the structural setting from the displayed potential, dimensions and numerical constants. The pushforward law of the square-integrable initial state has finite second moment by the mapped-measure characterization of square integrability. Apply the already proved sharp target-based parameter theorem to this initial law. The exact identity of the Gaussian recursion laws replaces its kernel-iterate law by the law of the original recursion. This proves the same improved bound in the original algorithm, with all potential assumptions and all distributional requirements displayed explicitly.

steps.title: Writing the discretization term explicitly
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(m>0\) and \(L,D\ge0\). Then

\[6\gamma\sqrt{\frac Lm\,LD}=\frac{6L}{\sqrt m}\sqrt D\,\gamma.\]

If also \(\gamma\ge0\), then

\[\frac{6L}{\sqrt m}\sqrt D\,\gamma=\frac{40}{11}\sqrt{m\gamma}\cdot\frac{33}{20}\frac Lm\sqrt D\sqrt\gamma,\]

and \(m\gamma\le121/1600\) implies \(\frac{6L}{\sqrt m}\sqrt D\,\gamma\le\frac{33}{20}\frac Lm\sqrt D\sqrt\gamma\).

Proof. Multiplying the left side of the first identity by \(\sqrt m\) gives \(6L\gamma\sqrt D\) by the earlier curvature scaling identity; divide by \(\sqrt m>0\). For the second identity write \(\sqrt{m\gamma}=\sqrt m\sqrt\gamma\), use \((\sqrt m)^2=m\), \((\sqrt\gamma)^2=\gamma\) and \(\frac{40}{11}\cdot\frac{33}{20}=6\). The inequality is the earlier factorized comparison with Project 03, rewritten by the first identity. Equivalently, \(\frac{40}{11}\sqrt{m\gamma}\le1\) exactly when \(m\gamma\le121/1600\).

steps.title: Ordering the curvature constants and the one-point space
steps.body:
Claim. If \(d_ heta+d_x>0\) and a differentiable joint potential \(U\) is \(m\)-strongly convex with an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, then \(m\le L\). On a one-point measurable space, any two probability measures are equal.

Proof. Take a unit coordinate vector \(v\). Strong monotonicity of the gradient, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and the Lipschitz bound give

\[m=m\|v\|^2\le\langle abla U(v)- abla U(0),v angle\le\| abla U(v)- abla U(0)\|\le L.\]

On a one-point space every set is empty or the whole space, where both probability measures take the values \(0\) and \(1\).

steps.title: Stationary laws of the Gaussian IPLA transition
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(T\) be the Gaussian IPLA transition on scaled-state laws, under the structural assumptions \(U_y\in C^2\), \(m\)-strong convexity with \(m>0\), an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(\gamma>0\) and \(\gamma L\le1\). Then \(T\) has a stationary probability law with finite second moment. If \(\widehat\Pi\) is the constructed invariant law, \(\Pi'\) is any stationary law with finite second moment, and \(\mu\) has finite second moment, then

\[W_2(\mu,\widehat\Pi)\le W_2(\mu,\Pi').\]

Proof. When \(d_\theta+d_x>0\), the previous step gives \(L\ge m>0\), and the invariant law constructed for the lifted chain is a stationary probability law with finite second moment. When \(d_\theta=d_x=0\), the state space is a point; its Dirac law is stationary because both it and its image are probability measures on a point. In this case every probability law is that same point mass, so all distances in the displayed comparison are zero.

For the remaining comparison suppose \(d_\theta+d_x>0\). Both stationary laws have finite second moments, so \(W_2(\Pi',\widehat\Pi)<\infty\). One step of synchronous contraction gives

\[W_2(\Pi',\widehat\Pi)=W_2(T\Pi',T\widehat\Pi)\le(1-m\gamma)\,W_2(\Pi',\widehat\Pi).\]

Here \(0\le1-m\gamma<1\) because \(m\gamma\le L\gamma\le1\). This forces \(W_2(\Pi',\widehat\Pi)=0\). The triangle inequality then gives \(W_2(\mu,\widehat\Pi)\le W_2(\mu,\Pi')+0\).
